theme: Unit 19 review, The New Covenant Applied, Acts
memoryText: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Jesus speaks these words to his disciples just before he ascends. They are his last words in Acts, and they set the agenda for the rest of the book and the church age.

“But you will receive power.” Jesus does not ask the disciples to do the work in their own strength. They will receive power. The power is not for show, but for witness.

“When the Holy Spirit has come upon you.” The source of the power is the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost. Without him there is no true witness. With him, ordinary people become bold.

“And you will be my witnesses.” A witness tells what he has seen and heard. The disciples had seen the risen Jesus. We have the testimony of Scripture and our own experience of grace. We too can tell what we know.

“In Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria.” The witness begins at home, in your city, then reaches the surrounding region and the despised outsiders. Each of us has a Jerusalem, a Judea, and a Samaria.

“And to the end of the earth.” There is no limit. The gospel is for every nation, and the church is called to carry it there.

When you feel inadequate to share the gospel, say this verse. The power is his, and the promise is for you.
unitRecap: You have read the book of Acts, the story of the risen Christ continuing his work by the Holy Spirit through his church. It began with the ascension, when Jesus promised power to witness in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth. In four doctrinal pauses, you studied Christ’s ascension and reign, the person and work of the Holy Spirit, repentance, and the means of grace. At Pentecost, the Spirit was poured out on all flesh, fulfilling Joel, Ezekiel, and Jeremiah, and Peter preached that God had made Jesus both Lord and Christ. The church devoted itself to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer. Despite arrests, the death of Stephen, and persecution, the word of God increased. It moved to Samaria, to an Ethiopian official, and to Cornelius, the first Gentile convert, when God showed Peter that no one is common or unclean. Saul, the persecutor, met the risen Christ and became Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles. The church at Antioch sent Barnabas and Paul on the first journey, the Jerusalem Council affirmed that Gentiles are saved by grace through faith, and the second and third journeys planted churches in Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth, and Ephesus, in line with the Abrahamic promise that all families of the earth would be blessed. Paul’s farewell to the Ephesian elders charged them to shepherd the church of God, and he went up to Jerusalem, was arrested, defended himself before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa, and was brought through storm and shipwreck to Rome, where he preached the kingdom of God with all boldness and without hindrance. The Psalms accompanied the story: Psalms 2, 16, and 110 for the exalted Christ, and Psalms 67, 87, 117, 96, 98, and 100 for the nations.

reviewQuestions.question: How does Pentecost fulfill the promises of Joel, Ezekiel, and Jeremiah?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Read Joel 2:28-32, Ezekiel 36:26-27, Jeremiah 31:33-34, and Acts 2:14-21. What did these prophets promise about the Spirit and the new covenant, and what do you see in Acts 2 that matches?

reviewQuestions.question: What does the Jerusalem Council decide?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Reread Acts 15:1-35. What was the question, how did Peter and James reason, and what was the result? Why does this matter for the gospel of grace?

reviewQuestions.question: How does Paul’s missionary strategy reflect the Abrahamic promise?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Think about Genesis 12:3 and Acts 13:47. Notice where Paul went first, how the Gentiles responded, and how he planted churches with elders. How does this show that the promise to bless all nations was being fulfilled?

reviewQuestions.question: What does Acts teach us about the nature of the church?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look at Acts 2:42-47 and 20:28. What are the marks of a healthy church? What does it mean that the church belongs to God, who obtained it with his own blood?

prayerPrompts: Thank God for the Spirit who empowers witnesses.
Thank him for how the gospel has reached you.
Ask him to keep the unit verse before you.
